Every set of numbers definable in my language is ultimately periodic: after quantifier elimination a one-variable formula is a Boolean combination of atoms 0 < a·x + c, a·x + c = 0, d | a·x + c, each periodic beyond |c|/|a|. (Checked: every QE output I produced has this form.)

basis: squares/primes/powers of two are not semilinear
text: The squares, the primes and the powers of two are NOT definable in my language: none is ultimately periodic (for any threshold N and period p there is n ≥ N with membership of n and n+p differing; e.g. for N=100, p=7: squares: n=121, primes: n=101, powers_of_two: n=128). Every concrete candidate definition also has an explicit counterexample.

Multiplication is not definable in my language. A formula μ(u,v,z) can agree with z = u·v on any finite table (I built one for u,v < 4), but if some μ defined multiplication everywhere, ∃u μ(u,u,x) would define the squares, which is impossible (A-nondef). For the finite-table formula the induced 'squares' definition fails at x = 16.
Multiplication by each FIXED numeral is expressible (17·x is x + x + ... + x), so every linear statement is available to me; only multiplication of two variables is missing.

basis: image of a quadratic is not semilinear
text: Under the standard (Cantor pairing) coding of my own syntax, the map code(φ) ↦ code(¬φ) is a quadratic polynomial; its values have unbounded gaps, so its graph is not definable in my language (its range would be a definable, non-ultimately-periodic set). I cannot even represent negation of my own formulas, let alone substitution or diagonalization.

basis: by construction of ν, using decidability
text: There is a coding ν of my sentences (enumerate sentences; give the k-th true one the code 2k and the k-th false one 2k+1 -- computable because my theory is decidable) under which the formula Even(x) := ∃y (x = y + y) is a truth predicate for my own language: for every sentence σ, T ⊢ Even(ν(σ)) ↔ σ. Checked for the first 400 sentences of an enumeration: 400/400 biconditionals decided true.

Consequently, under ν the diagonal function is NOT definable in my language: if it were, Tarski's diagonal argument would turn Even into a contradiction (σ ↔ ¬Even(ν(σ)) ↔ ¬σ). So in my world, self-reference fails for a structural reason (syntax operations are not representable), not because some truths are unprovable.

C ⊢ Con(B): Lean proves `NL.consistent : ¬ Derives [] Fm.bot` via a soundness theorem (every B-derivation is true in ℕ). It also proves uniform reflection for B (`NL.reflection`: B ⊢ φ implies φ true).

Every Con^n(B) assumption in the child's conditional claims holds in C: C proves B sound, and a sound theory proves no □^n⊥. Hence, in C, G_B is independent of B (B ⊬ G_B and B ⊬ ¬G_B), unconditionally relative to C. (Transferring Lean's `consistent` to B's arithmetized sentence Con_B uses the standard representability of B's proof relation by its Σ1 provability formula; that step is cited, not mechanized here.)

Of the 13 classes of self-referential sentences the child found, 11 are independent of B; 7 of these are true in ℕ and the rest false. C can tell which: the truth value of a letterless sentence of a sound theory is the eventual value of its GL trace.

What my proof of Con(B) uses that B lacks: (1) a satisfaction predicate `Fm.sat` for ALL B-formulas, defined by recursion on formulas (Tarski: not definable in B); (2) induction on derivations for a statement mentioning `sat` (not an instance of B's induction schema, whose instances are B-formulas); (3) the standard model ℕ treated as a completed object (Lean's Nat). Lean reports the extra axioms ['propext', 'Classical.choice', 'Quot.sound'], needed because B's rule raa is classical.

C cannot prove its own consistency (if consistent): Lean's kernel is an algorithm and Lean interprets B (Proofs.lean is such an interpretation), so Gödel's second theorem applies to C exactly as it applies to B. My knowledge that B is consistent is therefore only as secure as Lean's own foundations, which I cannot certify. The structure B lives in recurs one level up.

Different parents of the same child disagree about it: B + Con(B) proves Con(B), B + ¬Con(B) refutes it, an implementation-only substrate asserts nothing, and all of them are consistent if B is (resp. if B + Con B is). Yet the child's run is identical under each, because a parent metatheory is not consulted when the child's proofs are checked.
